Looking back later, Zhang Yuansheng could no longer say with certainty whether that paper should technically have been called a reporting certificate, a job assignment notice, or a transfer order.

In the mid-1990s, many young people’s first jobs carried a sense that paper could decide fate. School, work unit, personnel file, employment relationship—one layer connected to another until a recent graduate was finally sent to one particular place.
The exact name of the document did not matter very much.
What mattered was that it named a destination.
Shengli Oilfield.
Oilfield Construction Company No. 3.

Those words were not unfamiliar to Zhang Yuansheng. Since the age of twelve, his growing up had been tied to the oilfield. But this time was different. As a boy, he had come with his parents; after university, he was returning to the system under his own name.
The same place can look completely different when a person’s role has changed.

Before, his father went to work and he only knew that adults had adult business. Now that it was his own turn, he began to understand that “having a work unit” meant more than leaving in the morning and coming home in the afternoon. It meant that his personnel file would be received there, his wages would begin there, and the rest of his work history would be written from that point onward.
A person’s real entrance into society does not always come with a soundtrack.
No one stands at the door and announces: from today, the second stage of your life begins.
More often, it is only a sheet of paper, a stamp, and a date on which you are told to report.
Then you go.
Zhang Yuansheng went too.

He did not think of it as some dramatic turning point of destiny. For a young man in his twenties, graduating and having a job was simply something solid and reassuring. His parents could relax, and he could finally begin earning his own money.

The word “stability” in those years did not mean exactly what he would later hear it mean in Canada. It was not only stable income. It was more like a structure for an entire life: a work unit gathered many things under one roof, and people naturally imagined decades ahead as a continuous line.
From the first day of work, the future seemed to have acquired a rough outline.
Work, learn the job gradually; marry when the time came; have children; let the years move forward one after another.
There was nothing wrong with that.
In fact, it was precisely the life countless ordinary people worked hardest to build.

Zhang Yuansheng never thought there was anything shameful about being ordinary. Later, whether he was managing a warehouse, cleaning offices, or tinkering with his own software, he kept a plain standard: if a job needs doing, do it well. A position may not define a person, but the way a person treats a position slowly becomes part of his character.
At the time, none of that had yet become language in his mind.
What the man in his twenties saw was simply a working life about to begin for real.
The road from campus back to the oilfield was not unfamiliar. What was unfamiliar was his identity.
Before, when he came home, he was a student coming home.
This time, he was an employee reporting for duty.
The change was subtle enough that other people might not have noticed it. To him, however, it meant that from then on many things could no longer be casually filed under “we’ll deal with it later.”
Salary, responsibility, colleagues, supervisors, family—all would enter one after another.
Life was becoming concrete.

Many years later, he would notice that more than one piece of paper had appeared at the threshold of his life: immigration forms, house documents, employment contracts, Apple Developer approval emails, even the small word Pending on a computer screen. At one time or another, each had looked like a door.
A door does not walk for you.
It only tells you: you can go this way.
That piece of paper in 1995 was such a door.
It did not send him somewhere far away.
Instead, it sent him back into a familiar world.
But this time he was no longer someone’s child, no longer someone’s student.
He had his own employee number, his own place, and the beginning of his own responsibilities.
His student years truly ended there.
On the next page were four Chinese characters:
油建三公司—Oilfield Construction Company No. 3.
